clue.text: See 16
What can you see through the halo of a holy scrubber?

indicators.note: what you can see through the words is the run of letters showing across them

explanation.surface: Asking what shows through the halo of a saint who scrubs.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs through 'haLO OF A Holy'.
explanation.definitionFit: This dried gourd is used as a bath sponge for scrubbing the skin.

clue.text: Dwarf very quietly nestling in the dry grass

indicators.note: nestling in puts the quiet letters inside the grass word

parts.note: hay is dried grass
PP, pianissimo, is the musical direction for very quietly

explanation.surface: A dwarf nestles very quietly in the hay.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the seven dwarfs in Disney's Snow White carries this name.

clue.text: Pester porter about union coming to premature end

indicators.note: the drink word goes around the cut union word

parts.note: porter is a dark beer

indicators.note: ending early, the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a league is a union or alliance

explanation.surface: Someone harasses a hotel porter about a union that breaks up early.
explanation.walkthrough: Porter here is the dark drink, not a hotel doorman: 'about' wraps it around the shortened union word, which 'coming to premature end' trims of its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To besiege, and so to harass or pester persistently.

clue.text: London thoroughfare not entirely blessed by Vera Lynn?

indicators.note: only part of the song title is used, its opening word dropped

parts.note: Bless 'Em All was a wartime song sung by Vera Lynn

explanation.surface: A London street that Vera Lynn did not quite bless.
explanation.walkthrough: Vera Lynn was the Second World War's 'Forces' Sweetheart'. 'not entirely' removes BLESS from BLESS THEM ALL. The Mall is the avenue leading to Buckingham Palace.
explanation.definitionFit: The ceremonial road running from Trafalgar Square to Buckingham Palace in London.

clue.text: It's thrown out of eastern plane, one with cargo of cocaine

indicators.note: a plane with a cargo carries it inside, so the cocaine letter goes within the letters before it

parts.note: a jet is a type of plane
C is slang shorthand for cocaine
A, the indefinite article, means one

explanation.surface: Smuggling story: an eastern plane carrying cocaine has something tossed out of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Material hurled out of a volcano or explosion is called by this Latin-derived plural noun.

clue.text: The end of the opening match?

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

parts.note: a vent is an opening

explanation.surface: The final moments of the season's opening game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'end of' takes E from 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sporting contest, as at an athletics meeting, is an example of a match.

clue.text: Impressive dish unfinished: I'm over the cause of the disturbance

indicators.note: the impressive word says it sits over the next piece in this down clue

parts.note: epic means grand or impressive

indicators.note: unfinished means the last letter is removed

parts.note: an entree is a dish served at a meal

explanation.surface: An impressive dish left half-eaten causes a disturbance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfinished' cuts ENTREE to ENTRE, and 'I'm over' puts EPIC above it in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The point on the surface directly over an earthquake's source is where the disturbance centres.

clue.text: Doctor's aim: get train going west!

indicators.note: going west is slang for going wrong, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A doctor's goal: get the westbound train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going west' rearranges GET TRAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor aims at giving medical care to a patient.

clue.text: Maybe John's turn to enchant, briefly?

parts.note: a go is a turn in a game

indicators.note: said briefly, the word loses its final letter

parts.note: to spell is an old verb meaning to bewitch or enchant

explanation.surface: Is it now John's turn to cast a quick spell?
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' cuts the last L from SPELL, leaving SPEL.
explanation.definitionFit: John wrote one of the four New Testament accounts of Christ's life, so his book is an example.

clue.text: First person to mention vessel for cosmetic

indicators.note: to mention something is to say it, so the pronoun is taken for its spoken form

parts.note: I is the first-person singular pronoun
a liner is a large passenger ship

explanation.surface: The first one to bring up a ship is turning to make-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to mention' tells you that the pronoun I is heard as EYE.
explanation.definitionFit: This make-up product, applied as a line around the eyes, is a cosmetic.

clue.text: S American native finds top unknown horse to back

parts.note: a cap is a top or lid
Y is an unknown quantity in algebra

indicators.note: to go back means the horse word is read in reverse

parts.note: an Arab is a breed of horse

explanation.surface: A South American finds a hat with an unknown horse to bet on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to back' turns ARAB into ARAB backwards, ABARA; 'finds' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the largest living rodent, native to South America.

clue.text: Number left after the start of the year

indicators.note: the departure word is placed after the opening letter
the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: went is the past tense of leave, so left

explanation.surface: A number that has departed after the first of the year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start of' takes T from 'the'; WENT comes after it and Y (year) ends the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Twice ten is a cardinal number.

clue.text: Like word with two meanings, and big clue to anagrams?

indicators.note: the plural noun used as a verb tells you to rearrange the preceding words

explanation.surface: A word with two senses, and a hefty hint for solving anagrams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anagrams' rearranges AND BIG CLUE TO into the hyphenated answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something working in two ways at once, as a pun with two senses does, is described this way.

clue.text: Complete trademark at 9, employing computer's ultimate printing method

parts.note: to do is to complete

indicators.note: employing means taking on, so the final letter is held inside

parts.note: IX is nine in Roman numerals

indicators.note: ultimate means the last letter

explanation.surface: Completing a trademark at nine on the computer's final printing method.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimate' takes R from 'computer's', and 'employing' puts it inside ATIX.
explanation.definitionFit: A printer forming characters from a grid of small dots used this method.

clue.text: It starts in Italy at points to be negotiated after one

indicators.note: the rearranged letters come after the letter for one

parts.note: A means one

indicators.note: points to be negotiated are worked through, rearranged

explanation.surface: Something starting in Italy has points to negotiate after the first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be negotiated' rearranges AT POINTS.
explanation.definitionFit: This Italian appetiser starts a meal in Italy.

clue.text: No time at all to attack?

definitions.text: No time at all to attack?

parts.words: No time at all to attack?
parts.note: reads as a nil span of time, but also as the set moment a military assault begins

explanation.definitionFit: The scheduled moment for an operation to start, which sounds like a nil amount of time.

clue.text: 26 all in attendance herein for today's 3 6dn

definitions.text: 26 all in attendance herein for today's 3 6dn

parts.words: 26 all in attendance herein for today's 3 6dn
parts.note: 26 is the count of what every speller learns; all of them are present in this grid, a pangram marking the paper's celebration of its 26,000th puzzle

explanation.surface: A celebratory note that a full roll-call of twenty-six is present for today's joyful occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: The 3 and 6dn refer to HAPPY and EVENT: the grid contains every one of the 26 symbols from A to Z, to mark the Telegraph's 26,000th cryptic.
explanation.definitionFit: The set from A to Z numbers twenty-six, and every one of them appears somewhere in this grid.

clue.text: Secretly not daft, comprehending the question

indicators.note: comprehending means including, so the letters go inside
daft means crazy, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Secretly not so silly once the question is understood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'daft' rearranges NOT to ONT, and 'comprehending' puts THEQ inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: This informal phrase means quietly or in secret.

clue.text: Press cutting one in theatre's not initially seen

indicators.note: not initially means the first letter is removed

parts.note: a surgeon is one who cuts in an operating theatre

explanation.surface: A newspaper story about someone cutting in a theatre not seen at first.
explanation.walkthrough: The theatre is an operating theatre. 'not initially' removes the S.
explanation.definitionFit: To urge on is to press or encourage someone forward.

clue.text: The design of the lawmaker

definitions.meaning: a picture made of small coloured tiles or stones
relating to Moses, who brought the law from Sinai

explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a tiled design; the adjective means relating to Moses, the biblical lawgiver.

clue.text: Peevish, use bridge …

definitions.meaning: to go over a river by a bridge

explanation.definitionFit: Peevish means irritated; also, to go over a river by bridge.

clue.text: Parasite exercising power to spear Burns' hero

indicators.note: the anagram spears, going through the middle of, the hero's name

parts.note: Tam o' Shanter is the hero of Robert Burns's poem, so TAM

indicators.note: exercising puts the letters through their paces, rearranging them

explanation.surface: A parasite uses its power to impale a poet's hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exercising' rearranges POWER into PEWOR, and 'to spear' drives it through TAM. Robert Burns is Scotland's national poet.
explanation.definitionFit: This flat worm lives as a parasite in the gut of its host.

clue.text: … text for actor's libretto

definitions.meaning: the lines a performer sings or speaks

explanation.definitionFit: Words make up a text, and the lines of an opera or a part are its words.

clue.text: More of us dancing reel

indicators.note: dancing letters move about, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Several more of us are taking to the floor for a reel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dancing' rearranges MORE OF US.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish reel danced by four people is named after the group of four.

clue.text: This sound pierces!

parts.note: describes a piercing, high cry, and the closing mark itself is the printer's slang name for an exclamation mark

explanation.definitionFit: A piercing high-pitched cry, and also slang for the exclamation mark ending the clue.

clue.text: It's not theoretical: press relations ace backs what today goes after 12 and before …

parts.note: PR is short for public relations, the handling of the press
A is the abbreviation for ace in cards

indicators.note: backs means the number word is reversed

parts.words: what today goes after 12 and before
parts.note: today's puzzle is 26,000, so after 12 (TWENTY) comes six

explanation.surface: A practical PR ace backs whatever is happening today.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backs' reverses the number. Answer 12 is TWENTY and 26 is THOUSAND, so today's puzzle number, 26,000, supplies the number between them.
explanation.definitionFit: This means practice as opposed to theory.

clue.text: … this of our 20 22 seeing you on the beach!

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece on another means it comes before it

parts.note: thou is an archaic form of you
sand makes up the beach

explanation.surface: A holiday wish: seeing you on the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 and 22 are CROSS and WORDS: the paper has now published 26,000 of them. 'seeing' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The number completes twenty-six thousand, the count of Telegraph cryptics published.
